title: Alfred Adler: Individual Psychology
overview: Alfred Adler's individual psychology portrays people as unique, social and consciously goal-directed rather than driven by instincts and childhood events. Shaped by a sickly childhood in which he fought to overcome inferiority, Adler argued that universal inferiority feelings are the source of all striving through compensation; failure to compensate yields an inferiority complex (from organic inferiority, spoiling or neglect), while overcompensation yields a superiority complex. Our ultimate goal is striving for superiority or perfection, guided by fictional ideals (fictional finalism) and pursued through a unique style of life that we build with the creative power of the self. Social interest, an innate potential to cooperate, marks the healthy socially useful type, while dominant, getting and avoiding types lack it. Birth order shapes the style of life of first-born, second-born, youngest and only children. Adler assessed personality through birth order, early recollections and dream analysis, and later researchers developed social interest scales. Research supports many of his ideas, especially on early memories, neglect, pampering, social interest and first-borns, and his influence on later theorists is substantial despite charges of oversimplification.
objectives: Explain how Adler's individual psychology differs from Freud's psychoanalysis and how Adler's life shaped it.
Distinguish inferiority feelings, compensation, the inferiority complex and its three causes, and the superiority complex.
Explain striving for superiority (and the earlier masculine protest) and fictional finalism.
Describe the style of life, the creative power of the self and Adler's four basic styles of life.
Define social interest and explain the role of the mother and of Adler's life experiences in its development.
Describe Adler's views on first-born, second-born, youngest and only children.
Describe Adler's image of human nature and his assessment methods: early recollections, dream analysis and measures of social interest.
Summarise research on dreams, inferiority, early recollections, neglect, pampering, social interest and birth order, and evaluate Adler's contributions and criticisms.

sections.heading: Individual Psychology: Adler's Image of Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Alfred Adler built a theory of personality that refused to treat people as victims of instincts, biological drives or childhood events. He named it individual psychology because it centred on the uniqueness of every person, and because it rejected Freud's claim that all of us share the same universal biological motives and goals.

For Adler, a human being is first and foremost a social being. Personality is shaped by each person's particular social surroundings and relationships, not by the effort to satisfy biological needs. This leads to the main contrasts with Freud that examiners love to ask about. First, Freud gave sex a central role in personality formation; Adler played it down. Second, Freud placed the unconscious at the heart of personality; Adler placed the conscious mind there. Third, Freud saw behaviour as driven by forces we cannot see or control; Adler saw people as active agents who create their own unique selves and steer their own futures.

The chapter also points out how striking the contrast is when we remember the background the two men shared. They were only 14 years apart in age, grew up in the same city (Vienna) in the same era, and trained as physicians at the same university. Yet they produced sharply different pictures of human nature. As with Freud, the chapter suggests that parts of Adler's own childhood shaped the way he came to see people, which is why his life story is treated as an important key to the theory.

In short, individual psychology is a social, conscious, forward-looking and optimistic theory. Its main building blocks, developed in the rest of the chapter, are inferiority feelings and compensation, striving for superiority or perfection, fictional finalism, the style of life, the creative power of the self, social interest and birth order.
sections.simple: Adler called his theory individual psychology because it focuses on what makes each person unique. He saw people as social beings who consciously shape their own lives, and he gave much less importance to sex and the unconscious than Freud did.
keyPoints: Individual psychology = Adler's theory; stresses the uniqueness of each person.
Humans are primarily social beings shaped by social environment, not biological needs.
Adler minimised sex and put the conscious, not the unconscious, at the core of personality.
People actively create their selves and direct their futures.
Adler and Freud: 14 years apart, same city, era and medical school, yet very different theories.

sections.heading: The Life of Adler (1870-1937): Childhood and Adolescence
sections.detailed:
Adler's early years were dominated by illness, closeness to death and jealousy of his older brother, and the chapter presents them as a living example of his later theory.

Illness and death. He suffered from rickets, a vitamin D deficiency that softens the bones, which kept him from playing with other children. When he was 3, his younger brother died in the bed next to him. At 4 he nearly died of pneumonia himself, and on hearing the doctor tell his father that the boy was lost, he decided to become a doctor. This wish to defeat death later reappears as his own fictional final goal.

Family relations. His mother pampered him at first, but at the age of 2 he was suddenly dethroned by the birth of another baby. Biographers suggest she may then have rejected him, though he was clearly his father's favourite. This was the reverse of Freud's pattern (closer to his mother), and Adler found the Oedipus complex useless because it did not match his own childhood.

Sibling rivalry and compensation. Adler was always jealous of his healthy, athletic older brother, who could run and jump while every movement was a strain for Alfred. He felt inferior to his brother and to the neighbourhood children, and he resolved to work hard to overcome these feelings and compensate for his physical limits. Despite being small, clumsy and unattractive, he forced himself into games and sports, gradually gaining self-esteem and social acceptance. He developed a lifelong liking for the company of others. This is why his theory gives much more weight than Freud's to peers and siblings, and to relationships with children outside the family.

School. At the same school Freud had attended, Adler was at first unhappy and mediocre. A teacher, thinking him fit for nothing else, advised his father to apprentice him to a shoemaker, a prospect that frightened him. He was especially poor at mathematics, but through sheer hard work he rose from failing to the top of his class.

The chapter calls his childhood both a tragedy and a textbook case of his own theory: overcoming childhood weakness and inferiority to shape one's destiny. Adler himself said that anyone who knew his life would see how closely his childhood matched his ideas. This answers the review question on how his theory reflected his childhood: inferiority feelings, compensation, dethronement, sibling rivalry, the importance of peers, and rejection of the Oedipus complex all trace back to these years.
sections.simple: Adler was a sickly child with rickets who nearly died of pneumonia and was jealous of his healthy older brother. He fought his feelings of inferiority through effort, in sport and at school, which is exactly what his later theory describes.
keyPoints: Rickets, death of a younger brother (age 3), near-fatal pneumonia (age 4) - decided to become a doctor.
Pampered then dethroned at 2; father's favourite; rejected the Oedipus complex.
Jealous of healthy older brother; compensated by forcing himself into games and sports.
Peer and sibling relations became central to his theory.
Poor student told to become a shoemaker; worked his way to the top of the class.
His childhood is a textbook example of overcoming inferiority.

sections.heading: The Life of Adler: Adulthood, Relations with Freud, and Becoming a Celebrity in America
sections.detailed:
Adulthood. Fulfilling his childhood ambition, Adler studied medicine at the University of Vienna, though with only a mediocre record. He began in private practice as an eye specialist (ophthalmologist), moved into general medicine, and became interested in incurable diseases. His distress at being unable to prevent death, especially among young patients, pushed him to specialise in neurology and psychiatry.

Relations with Freud. In 1902 Freud invited Adler and three others to weekly discussions of psychoanalysis at his home, beginning a 9-year association. The two were never close, though Freud at first praised Adler's skill in gaining patients' trust. The chapter stresses that Adler was never Freud's student or disciple and was never analysed by him. A colleague of Freud's claimed Adler could not probe the unconscious, and the chapter wonders whether this is why Adler built his theory on the more accessible conscious mind. By 1910 Adler was president of the Vienna Psychoanalytical Society and coeditor of its journal, yet also a growing critic of Freud; he soon cut all ties with psychoanalysis.

The break was bitter. Freud mocked Adler's height (Adler was 5 inches shorter) and called him loathsome, abnormal, mad with ambition, venomous, paranoid, jealous and sadistic, and his theory worthless. Adler answered by calling Freud a swindler and psychoanalysis filth, and he became furious whenever he was introduced as Freud's student. In later life he became just as bitter toward defectors from his own school as Freud had been toward him, flaring up when his authority was challenged.

Becoming a celebrity in America. In 1912 Adler founded the Society for Individual Psychology. He served in the Austrian army in World War I (1914-1918) and afterwards organised government-sponsored child-counselling clinics in Vienna, where he introduced group training and guidance, forerunners of modern group therapy. He first visited the United States in 1926, giving hugely popular lectures, and moved to New York City in 1929. His geniality, optimism, warmth and strong ambition made him nationally known, and he became America's first popular psychologist. In 1937, during an exhausting 56-lecture tour of Europe, he died of a heart attack in Scotland.
sections.simple: Adler trained in medicine in Vienna and moved into psychiatry. He spent nine years in Freud's circle but was never his disciple, and the two split bitterly. He founded his own society in 1912, started child-guidance clinics, and became America's first celebrity psychologist before dying in 1937.
keyPoints: Medicine at University of Vienna; ophthalmology, then general medicine, then neurology and psychiatry.
9-year association with Freud from 1902; never a disciple or analysed by Freud.
1910: president of the Vienna Psychoanalytical Society, yet an open critic; then broke away.
Mutual hostility: Freud insulted Adler; Adler called Freud a swindler.
1912 Society for Individual Psychology; child-counselling clinics with group methods (forerunner of group therapy).
US from 1926, moved to New York 1929; America's first popular psychologist; died in Scotland, 1937.

sections.heading: Inferiority Feelings: The Source of All Human Striving
sections.detailed:
Inferiority feelings are the motor of Adler's whole system. He believed they are a constant motivating force behind all behaviour; to be human, in his phrase, is to feel inferior. Because everyone has them, inferiority feelings are not a sign of weakness or abnormality. They are the normal condition of all people.

Adler went further and called them the source of all human striving. Individual growth comes from compensation, our efforts to overcome real or imagined inferiorities. Throughout life we are pushed by the need to master this sense of inferiority and to strive toward ever higher levels of development. Compensation, defined in the margin as the motivation to overcome inferiority and reach higher development, is therefore the positive, healthy response to inferiority feelings.

Where do these feelings come from? Adler traced them to infancy. Infants are small, helpless and wholly dependent on adults. He believed infants are aware of their parents' greater size and strength, and of their own inability to resist or challenge that power. So they develop feelings of inferiority in relation to the bigger, stronger people around them.

An important point for exams: this early inferiority is universal, but it is not genetic. It arises from the environment, which happens to be the same for every infant: a climate of helplessness and dependence on adults. Inferiority feelings are therefore inescapable. More importantly, they are necessary, because without them there would be no motivation to strive and grow. This is a key difference from a purely pathological view: for Adler, feeling inferior is the starting point of all growth, and problems arise only when a person fails to compensate (the inferiority complex) or overcompensates (the superiority complex).
sections.simple: Adler believed everyone feels inferior, starting from the helplessness of infancy, and that this is normal. Trying to overcome these feelings (compensation) is what drives all growth and achievement.
keyPoints: Inferiority feelings are normal and universal, not a sign of weakness.
They are the source of all human striving.
Compensation = motivation to overcome inferiority and reach higher development.
They begin in infancy from helplessness and dependence on adults.
Caused by the shared infant environment, not by genetics; inescapable and necessary.

sections.heading: The Inferiority Complex and Its Causes
sections.detailed:
What if a child fails to compensate for normal inferiority feelings? Then the feelings intensify and an inferiority complex develops. People with this complex hold a poor opinion of themselves and feel helpless and unable to cope with life's demands. Adler found such a complex in the childhood of many adults who came to him for treatment. The key distinction: inferiority feelings are normal and motivating; the inferiority complex is what results when compensation fails.

Adler named three childhood sources of an inferiority complex.

1. Organic inferiority. Defective organs or body parts shape personality through the person's efforts to compensate for the defect, just as Adler compensated for his rickets. A physically weak child may focus on that weakness and work to develop superior athletic ability. The chapter gives historical examples: the Greek statesman Demosthenes overcame a stutter to become a great orator, and the sickly Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th US president, became a model of physical fitness. Adler's Vienna office was near an amusement park, and his patients included circus performers and gymnasts who had often built extraordinary skills by working to overcome childhood disabilities. Such efforts can produce striking artistic, athletic and social achievements, but if they fail, they can produce an inferiority complex.

2. Spoiling (pampering). Spoiled children are the centre of attention at home; every need and whim is met and little is refused. They naturally come to believe they are the most important people in any situation and that others should give way to them. School comes as a shock, because they are no longer the focus. They have little social feeling, are impatient with others, have never learned to wait, to overcome difficulties or to adjust to others' needs. When something blocks their gratification, they conclude that some personal deficiency must be holding them back, and an inferiority complex develops.

3. Neglect. Neglected, unwanted and rejected children grow up without love and security because their parents are indifferent or hostile. They develop feelings of worthlessness, sometimes anger, and view others with distrust. The chapter adds that neglect is now considered a major form of child abuse (Hickman, 2009).

These three causes link directly to later topics: neglect shapes a revenge-seeking style of life, and research later tests the effects of both pampering and neglect.
sections.simple: When a person cannot overcome normal inferiority feelings, they grow into an inferiority complex: a poor self-image and a sense of helplessness. Adler said it comes from three childhood sources: a physical weakness, being spoiled, or being neglected.
keyPoints: Inferiority complex = failure to compensate for normal inferiority feelings; poor self-opinion, helplessness.
Three sources: organic inferiority, spoiling, neglect.
Organic inferiority: compensation for a bodily defect (Demosthenes, Theodore Roosevelt, circus performers).
Spoiled children expect others to defer; school is a shock; they blame a personal deficiency.
Neglected children feel worthless, angry and distrustful; neglect is now seen as child abuse.

sections.heading: The Superiority Complex
sections.detailed:
Whatever the source of an inferiority complex, a person may try to overcompensate and so develop what Adler called a superiority complex: an exaggerated opinion of one's own abilities and accomplishments.

The chapter describes two forms. Some people with a superiority complex feel inwardly smug and superior and see no need to prove it through actual achievement. Others do feel such a need and work very hard to become extremely successful. In both forms, the person tends toward boasting, vanity, self-centredness and putting others down.

It is important to separate three ideas that sound alike. Inferiority feelings are normal and motivate growth. The inferiority complex comes from failing to compensate. The superiority complex comes from overcompensating. None of these is the same as striving for superiority, which Adler described as the healthy, universal urge toward perfection or completeness. A favourite exam question (review question 4) asks how the superiority complex differs from striving for superiority: the complex is an inflated self-image with boasting and contempt for others, whereas striving for superiority is not about being better than others at all but about completing and perfecting oneself.
sections.simple: A superiority complex is overcompensation for feeling inferior: the person has an inflated view of their own abilities. They tend to boast, be vain and self-centred, and look down on others.
keyPoints: Superiority complex = overcompensation for inferiority feelings.
Exaggerated opinion of one's abilities and accomplishments.
May involve no real achievement, or driven hard work toward success.
Marked by boasting, vanity, self-centredness and denigrating others.
Not the same as striving for superiority.

sections.heading: Striving for Superiority, or Perfection
sections.detailed:
If inferiority feelings are the source of motivation, what is the goal? Adler believed we strive for more than just getting rid of inferiority feelings, but his view of the ultimate goal changed over his career.

Early view: masculine protest and power. At first Adler linked inferiority with a general feeling of weakness or femininity, reflecting the low social status of women in his time. Compensating for this feeling he called the masculine protest. Its goal was a will or drive toward power in which aggression, then seen as a masculine trait, played a large part.

Later view: superiority or perfection. Adler later dropped the equation of inferiority with femininity and broadened his view: we strive for superiority, or perfection. He called this striving the fundamental fact of life (Adler, 1930), and superiority the ultimate goal toward which we move.

He did not mean superiority in the everyday sense, and the idea has nothing to do with the superiority complex. Striving for superiority is not trying to be better than everyone else, nor an arrogant, domineering tendency, nor an inflated self-image. It is a drive for perfection. The word perfection comes from a Latin word meaning to complete or finish, so we strive in order to perfect ourselves, to become complete or whole.

Future orientation. This innate drive toward wholeness looks to the future. Freud held that behaviour is determined by the past, by instincts and childhood experiences. Adler saw motivation in terms of expectations and aspirations for the future. He argued that instincts and primal impulses cannot explain personality; only the final goal of superiority or perfection can.

Two further points (p. 114). First, striving for superiority increases tension rather than reducing it. Unlike Freud, Adler did not believe our sole motive is tension reduction; striving for perfection demands great energy and effort, the opposite of a tension-free equilibrium. Second, striving occurs both in the individual and in society. As social beings we strive for perfection as members of a group as well, trying to perfect our culture. Individuals and society are interdependent, and people must work constructively with others for the good of all.

How we pursue this goal in daily life is answered by the concept of the style of life.
sections.simple: Adler said our main goal in life is to strive for superiority, meaning perfection or completeness, not being better than others. This goal pulls us toward the future, raises rather than lowers tension, and is pursued both individually and as members of society.
keyPoints: Early idea: masculine protest, a drive for power and aggression (inferiority equated with femininity).
Later idea: striving for superiority or perfection is the fundamental fact of life.
Superiority here means completion or wholeness (Latin root: to complete), not beating others.
Future-oriented, unlike Freud's past-determined view.
Striving increases tension, unlike Freud's tension reduction.
Pursued by both individuals and society; individual and society are interdependent.

sections.heading: Fictional Finalism
sections.detailed:
Adler used the term finalism for the idea that we have an ultimate goal, a final state of being, and a need to move toward it. But these goals are potentialities, not actualities: ideals that exist in us subjectively. Adler called them fictional or imagined ideals because they cannot be tested against reality. Examples given in the chapter are beliefs that all people are created equal or that all people are basically good.

Adler's own life illustrates the idea. His life goal was to conquer the death he had faced from pneumonia at age 4. His way of striving toward it was to become a physician. The goal is fictional because death can never ultimately be defeated, yet it guided his life choices.

Such beliefs shape how we perceive and treat others. For instance, if we believe certain behaviour will be rewarded in heaven or an afterlife, we act accordingly. Belief in an afterlife does not rest on objective reality, but it is real to the believer and it guides behaviour.

Adler formalised this as fictional finalism: the idea that fictional ideas guide our behaviour as we strive toward a complete or whole state of being. We direct our lives by many such fictions, but the most pervasive is the ideal of perfection, and Adler suggested that the best formulation of that ideal humans have reached so far is the concept of God. Adler himself preferred the terms subjective final goal or guiding self-ideal, but the concept is still known as fictional finalism (Watts & Holden, 1994).

Link to striving for superiority (review question 5): striving for superiority is the motive, and fictional finalism names the kind of goal it aims at. Perfection is never fully reachable or provable, so it is a fiction, yet it is the guiding ideal that pulls behaviour toward the future.
sections.simple: Fictional finalism means we are guided by imagined goals that cannot be tested against reality, such as the belief that all people are equal or that there is an afterlife. The most important of these fictions is the ideal of perfection, which steers our striving.
keyPoints: Finalism: we have an ultimate goal and a need to move toward it.
Goals are subjective, imagined ideals that cannot be tested against reality.
Adler's fictional goal: to conquer death, pursued by becoming a physician.
Most pervasive fiction = ideal of perfection; best formulation so far = the concept of God.
Adler preferred 'subjective final goal' or 'guiding self-ideal'.

sections.heading: The Style of Life
sections.detailed:
Everyone's ultimate goal is superiority or perfection, but each of us pursues it differently. Each person develops a unique pattern of characteristics, behaviours and habits, which Adler called a distinctive character or style of life. The margin definition adds that basic styles include the dominant, getting, avoiding and socially useful types.

How it develops. To understand the style of life we return to inferiority feelings and compensation. Infants feel inferior and are motivated to compensate for their helplessness and dependence. In compensating, they acquire a set of behaviours. A sickly child, for example, might try to build physical strength by running or lifting weights. These behaviours become part of the style of life, which is therefore a pattern of behaviour designed to compensate for inferiority.

What it does. Everything we do is shaped by our style of life. It decides which parts of the environment we attend to or ignore and which attitudes we hold. It becomes the guiding framework for all later behaviour.

When it forms. The style of life is learned from social interactions and is so firmly crystallised by age 4 or 5 that it is difficult to change afterwards. Its nature depends on social interactions, especially the person's birth order and the nature of the parent-child relationship.

An example from neglect. Neglected children may feel unable to cope with life's demands and become distrustful and hostile. Their style of life may then involve seeking revenge, resenting others' success and grabbing whatever they feel they are owed.

This early fixing of the style of life raises an apparent problem: it seems almost as deterministic as Freud's view. Adler's answer is the creative power of the self.
sections.simple: The style of life is each person's unique way of striving for perfection, built from the ways they learned to compensate for inferiority as a child. It is formed through social experiences, especially birth order and parenting, and is largely fixed by age 4 or 5.
keyPoints: Style of life = unique pattern of characteristics, behaviours and habits by which we strive for perfection.
Grows out of childhood compensation for inferiority.
Shapes what we notice, ignore and the attitudes we hold.
Learned through social interactions; crystallised by age 4-5.
Depends especially on birth order and the parent-child relationship.
Neglect can produce a revengeful, resentful style of life.

sections.heading: The Creative Power of the Self
sections.detailed:
There seems to be a contradiction in Adler's theory. He said we control our fate and are not its victims, yet he also said the style of life is fixed by social relationships in the first few years and changes little afterwards. That sounds almost as deterministic as Freud's emphasis on early childhood. Adler resolved the dilemma with the concept of the creative power of the self, defined in the margin as the ability to create an appropriate style of life.

We create ourselves. Adler believed we create our selves, our personality, our character, terms he used interchangeably with style of life. We are not passively moulded by childhood experiences. What matters is not the experiences themselves but our conscious attitude toward them. Neither heredity nor environment fully explains personality. Instead, the way we perceive and interpret these influences is the basis on which we creatively build our attitude toward life.

Free will. Adler believed in individual free will, which lets each person create an appropriate style of life out of the abilities and experiences supplied by genetic endowment and social environment. Heredity and environment are the building materials; the creative self is the builder. Adler was vague about the specifics of how this happens, but he insisted that our style of life is not determined for us: we are free to choose and create it. Once it has been created, however, the style of life remains constant throughout life.

This concept answers review question 6: according to Adler, people play an active, not a passive, role in developing the self. It is also the main reason Adler's theory is seen as less deterministic and more optimistic than Freud's. The chapter later notes, as a criticism, that it is unclear how a young child could make such momentous choices before age 5.
sections.simple: Adler said we are not just products of our genes and upbringing. We use those as raw material and actively create our own style of life through how we interpret our experiences, which is what makes his theory less deterministic than Freud's.
keyPoints: Resolves the apparent determinism of an early-fixed style of life.
Creative power of the self = ability to create an appropriate style of life.
Our conscious attitude to experiences matters more than the experiences themselves.
Heredity and environment provide materials; free will builds the style of life.
Once created, the style of life stays constant; Adler was unclear on the specifics.

sections.heading: Four Basic Styles of Life
sections.detailed:
Adler grouped life's universal problems into three categories: problems of behaviour toward others, problems of occupation, and problems of love. He proposed four basic styles of life for dealing with them.

1. The dominant (ruling) type shows a dominant or ruling attitude with little social awareness and acts without regard for others. The more extreme members attack others and become sadists, delinquents or sociopaths. The less virulent become alcoholics, drug addicts or suicides, believing they hurt others by attacking themselves.

2. The getting type expects to receive satisfaction from other people and so becomes dependent on them. Adler considered this the most common human type.

3. The avoiding type makes no attempt to face life's problems. By avoiding difficulties, the person avoids any chance of failure.

These three types are not prepared to cope with everyday problems. They cannot cooperate with others, and the clash between their style of life and the real world leads to abnormal behaviour, expressed as neuroses and psychoses. What they lack is what Adler came to call social interest.

4. The socially useful type, by contrast, cooperates with others and acts in line with their needs. Such people cope with problems within a well-developed framework of social interest. This is the healthy type and the one identified with social interest (review question 8).
sections.simple: Adler described four ways people deal with problems of relationships, work and love: dominating others, depending on others (getting), dodging problems (avoiding), or cooperating with others (socially useful). Only the socially useful type is healthy, because it has social interest.
keyPoints: Three problem areas: behaviour toward others, occupation, love.
Dominant type: ruling attitude, little social awareness; extreme forms sadists, delinquents, sociopaths.
Getting type: depends on others for satisfaction; the most common type.
Avoiding type: avoids problems to avoid failure.
First three lack social interest and may develop neuroses and psychoses.
Socially useful type: cooperates, has well-developed social interest.

sections.heading: Social Interest
sections.detailed:
Adler believed that getting along with others is the first task we meet in life. How well we manage it becomes part of our style of life and so affects how well we handle all of life's problems. He called this social interest: the individual's innate potential to cooperate with others to achieve personal and societal goals. His original German term, Gemeinschaftsgefuhl, is best translated as community feeling (Stepansky, 1983), but social interest is the accepted English term.

Innate potential, social development. Adler held that we are shaped more by social than by biological forces, yet the potential for social interest is innate. In that limited sense his approach has a biological element. However, how far this innate potential develops depends on early social experiences. So social interest is inborn as a potential but realised through experience.

Why it matters. No one can completely avoid other people or obligations to them. Since earliest times people have gathered in families, tribes and nations, because communities are essential for protection and survival. It has therefore always been necessary to cooperate with others. To reach both personal and communal goals the individual must cooperate with and contribute to society. Adler believed people have a fundamental need to belong in order to be healthy and well-functioning (Ferguson, 2010).

Social interest is the yardstick of psychological health in Adler's system: the three unhealthy styles of life lack it, while the socially useful type has it. Later research using the Social Interest Scale and Social Interest Index links high social interest to better mental and physical well-being.
sections.simple: Social interest is our inborn potential to cooperate with others for personal and social goals (Adler's German term means community feeling). The potential is innate, but whether it develops depends on early social experiences, and it is the mark of a healthy personality.
keyPoints: Getting along with others is life's first task.
Social interest = innate potential to cooperate with others to reach personal and societal goals.
German term Gemeinschaftsgefuhl = community feeling.
Potential is innate (a limited biological element); its development depends on early social experience.
Communities are needed for survival; people have a fundamental need to belong.

sections.heading: The Role of the Mother and of Adler's Life Experiences in Developing Social Interest
sections.detailed:
The role of the mother. The mother is the first person a baby meets, and through her behaviour she can either foster or block the growth of social interest. Adler thought her role was vital not only for social interest but for every aspect of personality. He wrote that the bond between mother and child is so close and far-reaching that no later characteristic can be called simply inherited, because the mother has adapted, trained and reshaped every inherited tendency; her skill or lack of it affects all the child's potential (quoted in Grey, 1998).

The mother must teach the child three things: cooperation, companionship and courage. Only children who feel a kinship with others can act courageously in coping with life's demands. Children, and later adults, who view others with suspicion and hostility approach life the same way. People with no social interest may become neurotics or even criminals. Adler traced a whole range of social evils, from war and racial hatred to public drunkenness, to a lack of community feeling. This answers review question 8 on which parental behaviours foster social interest.

The role of Adler's life experiences. Adler's own ideas about motivation changed with his circumstances. Early in his career, while he was struggling to establish his point of view inside Freud's circle, he argued that people are driven by a lust for power and a need to dominate. After breaking with Freud and gaining recognition, he changed his position and said people are motivated more by social interest than by power and dominance.

His personality changed in parallel. In Freud's group he was seen as cantankerous and ambitious, quarrelling over who had thought of ideas first. In later years he mellowed, and his system shifted from power and dominance to the gentler force of social or community interest. The chapter offers this as another example of how Adler's theory mirrored his own life.
sections.simple: The mother is the first and most important influence on social interest; she must teach cooperation, companionship and courage. Adler's own focus moved from power to social interest as he himself mellowed after leaving Freud's circle.
keyPoints: Mother is the first contact and can foster or thwart social interest.
Mother must teach cooperation, companionship and courage.
Lack of social interest linked to neurosis, crime, war, racial hatred and public drunkenness.
Early Adler: lust for power and need to dominate; later: social interest.
The shift mirrored Adler's own move from cantankerous ambition to a mellower personality.

sections.heading: Birth Order
sections.detailed:
One of Adler's most lasting contributions is the idea that birth order is a major social influence in childhood, one from which we create our style of life. Siblings share parents and a home, but they do not share identical social environments. Being older or younger than one's siblings, and being exposed to different parental attitudes, create different childhood conditions that help produce different kinds of personality.

Adler enjoyed amazing lecture audiences and dinner guests by correctly guessing people's birth order from their behaviour. He wrote about four situations: the first-born child, the second-born child, the youngest child and the only child. Each is examined in the sections that follow.

Birth order is also one of Adler's three main methods of assessment, alongside early recollections and dream analysis, and it is the most heavily researched of his ideas. An important qualification, stated at the end of the birth-order discussion, is that Adler was not proposing firm rules: position in the family makes certain styles of life more likely, but the creative self uses both birth order and early social interactions in constructing the style of life.
sections.simple: Adler said birth order is a big social influence on personality, because siblings grow up in different family situations even in the same home. He described four positions: first-born, second-born, youngest and only child.
keyPoints: Birth order is a major social influence from which we create our style of life.
Siblings do not share identical social environments.
Different positions and parental attitudes create different personalities.
Four situations: first-born, second-born, youngest, only child.
Adler liked to guess people's birth order from their behaviour.

sections.heading: The First-Born Child: Dethronement and Characteristics
sections.detailed:
A unique and enviable position, for a while. Parents are usually delighted with their first child and devote a great deal of time and attention to the new baby. First-borns get instant, undivided attention and live a happy, secure existence until the second child arrives.

Dethronement. Suddenly the first-born is no longer the centre of attention or the receiver of constant love and care; in a sense, they are dethroned. Affection and attention must now be shared. They must often wait until the newborn's needs are met and are told to be quiet so as not to disturb the baby. No one could expect them to accept this drastic displacement without a fight. They try to regain their former position of power and privilege, but the battle is lost from the start: things will never be the same. For a time they may become stubborn, badly behaved and destructive and refuse to eat or go to bed. They strike out in anger, but parents strike back with more powerful weapons. Punishment looks like further proof of their fall, and they may come to hate the second child who caused it.

Two factors affect the size of the shock. All first-borns feel it, but those who were excessively pampered feel a greater loss. And the older the first-born when the rival arrives, the less dethronement they experience: an 8-year-old will be less upset than a 2-year-old.

Characteristics. Adler found first-borns often oriented toward the past, locked in nostalgia and pessimistic about the future. Having once tasted power, they remain concerned with it all their lives. They can exercise power over younger siblings, but they are also more subject to parental power because more is expected of them.

There are advantages too. As the children grow, first-borns often act as teacher, tutor, leader and disciplinarian, expected to help care for younger siblings. This often helps them mature intellectually further than younger siblings. Zajonc (2001) explained that by answering younger siblings' questions and explaining word meanings, first-borns rehearse and articulate knowledge and so gain verbal fluency more quickly.

Adler also believed first-borns take an unusual interest in maintaining order and authority. They become good organisers, conscientious and careful about detail, and authoritarian and conservative in attitude. Adler described Freud, a first-born, as a typical eldest son. On the negative side, first-borns may grow up insecure and hostile, and Adler believed neurotics, perverts and criminals were often first-borns.
sections.simple: First-borns are the centre of attention until a sibling arrives and dethrones them, which is a painful shock they can never fully undo. Adler saw them as past-oriented, concerned with power, order and authority, and often intellectually ahead from tutoring younger siblings, but also at risk of insecurity and hostility.
keyPoints: First-borns enjoy undivided attention until dethroned by the second child.
Dethronement: attempts to regain position fail; may become stubborn and destructive and hate the sibling.
Pampered first-borns and younger first-borns (2 vs 8 years) feel the loss more.
Past-oriented, nostalgic, pessimistic; lifelong concern with power.
Tutoring role brings intellectual and verbal advantages (Zajonc).
Good organisers, conscientious, authoritarian and conservative; Freud as typical eldest son; may be insecure, hostile.

sections.heading: The Second-Born Child
sections.detailed:
Second-borns are also in a unique position. They never enjoy the powerful position the first-born once held, and even if another child is born later, they do not feel the dethronement experienced by first-borns.

By this time, parents have usually changed their child-rearing attitudes. A second baby is no novelty, so parents may be less anxious about their own behaviour and take a more relaxed approach.

From the start, second-borns have a pacesetter: the older sibling, whose behaviour serves as a model, a threat or a source of competition. Adler himself was a second-born with a lifelong competitive relationship with his older brother, whose name was Sigmund. Even as a famous analyst, Adler felt overshadowed; in middle age he wearily remarked that his wealthy businessman brother had always been ahead of him and still was (Hoffman, 1994).

Characteristics. Competition with the first-born may motivate the second-born to catch up and overtake the older sibling, which spurs language and motor development. Never having held power, second-borns are less concerned with it. They are more optimistic about the future and likely to be competitive and ambitious, as Adler was.

Less favourable outcomes are possible. If the older sibling excels in sport or study, the second-born may feel they can never surpass them and give up. Then competitiveness does not become part of their style of life, and they may become underachievers, performing below their ability in many areas of life.
sections.simple: Second-borns never hold the first-born's powerful position, and they get more relaxed parents. They have an older sibling to chase, which can make them optimistic, competitive and ambitious, but if the older sibling seems unbeatable they may give up and underachieve.
keyPoints: Never experience the first-born's power or its dethronement.
Parents are usually more relaxed with a second child.
Older sibling is a pacesetter: model, threat or competitor.
Adler, a second-born, competed all his life with brother Sigmund.
Typically optimistic, competitive and ambitious; competition spurs language and motor development.
If the older sibling seems unbeatable, may become an underachiever.

sections.heading: The Youngest Child
sections.detailed:
Youngest or last-born children never face the shock of being dethroned by another child. They often become the pet of the family, especially if their siblings are several years older.

Driven by the need to surpass their older siblings, youngest children often develop remarkably fast, and as adults last-borns are often high achievers in whatever work they take on.

The opposite can also happen. If youngest children are excessively pampered and come to believe they never need to learn to do anything for themselves, they may keep the helplessness and dependency of childhood as they grow older. Unused to striving and struggling, and used to being looked after, they find adjustment to adulthood difficult. This prediction is later linked to research on last-borns and alcoholism and binge drinking.
sections.simple: Youngest children are never dethroned and are often the family pet. The urge to catch up with older siblings can make them fast developers and high achievers, but if they are over-pampered they may stay dependent and struggle as adults.
keyPoints: Never dethroned; often the pet of the family.
Need to surpass older siblings speeds development.
Often high achievers as adults.
Excessive pampering can leave them helpless and dependent.
Pampered last-borns may find adult adjustment difficult.

sections.heading: The Only Child
sections.detailed:
Only children never lose their position of primacy and power in the family; they remain the focus and centre of attention. Because they spend more time with adults than children with siblings do, they often mature early and show adult behaviour and attitudes.

Problems may appear outside the home, for example at school, when only children discover they are no longer the centre of attention. They have learned neither to share nor to compete. If their abilities do not win them enough recognition and attention, they are likely to feel keenly disappointed. This covers review question 11: the advantages are early maturity and adult-like attitudes; the disadvantages are an inability to share or compete and disappointment when they are not the centre of attention.

A caution about all birth-order positions. Adler was not proposing firm rules of development. A child will not automatically acquire a particular character just from his or her position in the family. What Adler suggested was the likelihood that certain styles of life will develop as a function of birth order combined with early social interactions. The creative self uses both influences in constructing the style of life.
sections.simple: Only children stay the centre of attention and, spending time with adults, often mature early. But they never learn to share or compete, so they can be disappointed when school and life do not treat them as special. Adler stressed that birth order makes styles of life likely, not certain.
keyPoints: Never lose primacy; remain the centre of attention.
Time with adults leads to early maturity and adult attitudes.
Shock outside the home (e.g., school) when no longer the centre.
Have learned neither to share nor to compete; disappointed if not recognised.
Birth order gives likelihoods, not firm rules; the creative self combines it with social interactions.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Adler's system offers a hopeful, flattering image of human nature, the direct opposite of what the chapter calls Freud's dreary, pessimistic view. It is more satisfying to our sense of self-worth to see ourselves as able to consciously shape our development and destiny than to see ourselves as ruled by instincts and childhood experiences we cannot control.

Free will versus determinism. Adler's image is optimistic because he held that people are not driven by unconscious forces. We have the free will to shape the social forces that influence us and to use them creatively to construct a unique style of life.

Uniqueness versus universality. Uniqueness is another flattering aspect of Adler's view. Freud's system, by contrast, offered a depressing universality and sameness in human nature.

Nature versus nurture. Adler accepted that some aspects of human nature are innate, for example the potential for social interest and the striving for perfection. But experience determines how these inherited tendencies are realised. So both play a part, with experience decisive.

Importance of the past. Childhood influences matter, especially birth order and interactions with parents, but we are not victims of our childhood. We use childhood experiences to create our style of life.

Optimism. Adler saw each person as striving for perfection and viewed humanity in the same way. He believed in the creative power of the individual and was optimistic about social progress.

This section answers review question 14 on how Adler's image of human nature differs from Freud's: conscious rather than unconscious, free rather than determined, unique rather than universal, future-oriented rather than past-bound, and optimistic rather than pessimistic.
sections.simple: Adler's view of people is hopeful: we have free will, we are each unique, and we use our childhood experiences rather than being trapped by them. Some tendencies are inborn, but experience decides how they turn out, and Adler was optimistic about both individuals and society.
keyPoints: Hopeful, flattering view - the antithesis of Freud's pessimism.
Free will: people are not driven by unconscious forces.
Uniqueness rather than Freud's universality.
Some innate potentials (social interest, striving for perfection), realised through experience.
Childhood matters, but we are not its victims.
Optimistic about individuals and social progress.

sections.heading: Assessment in Adler's Theory
sections.detailed:
Like Freud, Adler built his theory by analysing patients: evaluating what they said and how they behaved during therapy. But his style was much more relaxed. Freud's patients lay on a couch with Freud sitting behind them; Adler and his patients sat facing each other in comfortable chairs, and sessions were more like chats between friends.

Humour. Adler liked to use humour, sometimes teasing patients in a friendly way. He kept a store of jokes suited to various neuroses and believed a joke could help a patient see how ridiculous the illness was. The chapter gives the example of an adolescent who felt guilty about masturbating; Adler joked that doing one or the other would be enough, but both was too much (Hoffman, 1994).

Observing the body. Adler observed everything: how patients walked and sat, how they shook hands, even which chair they chose. He believed the way we use our bodies reveals something about our style of life. Even sleeping position was revealing: restless sleepers and those who sleep flat on their backs want to seem more important than they are; sleeping on the stomach indicates a stubborn, negative personality; curling into the fetal position shows fear of interacting with others; and sleeping with arms outstretched shows a need to be nurtured and supported.

The entrance gates to mental life. Adler's primary assessment methods, which he called the entrance gates to mental life, are order of birth, early recollections and dream analysis. In addition, later psychologists developed tests based on social interest.

Purpose. The aim of assessment was to discover the patient's style of life and to judge whether it was the most appropriate one for that person. This section, with the next three, answers review question 15 on how Adler assessed his patients.
sections.simple: Adler's therapy was informal: face-to-face chairs, friendly chats and jokes. He read personality from body language and even sleeping positions, and his main tools were birth order, early recollections and dream analysis, all aimed at uncovering the person's style of life.
keyPoints: Face-to-face, informal sessions, unlike Freud's couch.
Used humour to help patients see how ridiculous their sickness was.
Observed posture, walk, handshake, chair choice and sleeping position.
Entrance gates to mental life: birth order, early recollections, dream analysis.
Goal: discover the style of life and judge if it is appropriate.

sections.heading: Early Recollections and Adler's Strange Early Memory
sections.detailed:
Adler held that personality is created in the first 4 or 5 years of life, and that our early recollections, memories from that period, reveal the style of life that continues to characterise us as adults. The margin defines early recollections as an assessment technique in which our earliest memories, whether of real events or fantasies, are assumed to reveal the primary interest of our life.

Real or fantasy does not matter. Adler found it made little difference whether a client's early memory was true or imagined. Either way, the person's primary life interest revolved around the remembered incident, so early recollections are considered the most satisfactory single indicators of lifestyle (Manaster & Mays, 2004). He also found that many early memories referred to actual physical objects (Clark, 2009).

Common themes. Although each memory should be interpreted in the context of the person's style of life, Adler noticed commonalities. Memories of danger or punishment suggested a tendency toward hostility. Memories of a sibling's birth showed a continuing sense of dethronement. Memories focused on one parent showed a preference for that parent. Memories of misbehaviour served as a warning against repeating it.

Adler versus Freud on memory. According to Kopp and Eckstein (2004), Adler believed people remember from early childhood only images that confirm their current view of themselves and the world, and only memories that support their direction of striving for significance and security. His approach therefore stresses what is remembered (selective memory and lifestyle), whereas Freud's stresses what is forgotten through repression.

Adler's strange early memory. At age 5, newly started at school, Adler remembered being terrified every day because his route to school went through a cemetery, while other children did not seem to notice it. Being the only frightened one deepened his sense of inferiority. One day he decided to end his fear and ran through the cemetery a dozen times until he felt he had conquered it; after that he walked to school without fear. Thirty years later he asked a former schoolmate whether the cemetery was still there and was told there had never been one. Other classmates said the same. Adler accepted that the memory was false, yet it symbolised the fear and inferiority, and the effort to overcome them, that characterised his style of life. The recollection had revealed an important aspect of his personality, which is exactly what review question 16 asks for.
sections.simple: Adler believed our earliest memories, true or imagined, reveal our style of life. His own vivid memory of conquering his fear of a cemetery on the way to school turned out to be false, yet it perfectly captured his lifelong pattern of overcoming inferiority.
keyPoints: Personality created in first 4-5 years; early recollections reveal the lifelong style of life.
Whether real or fantasy makes little difference; 'most satisfactory single indicators of lifestyle'.
Themes: danger/punishment = hostility; sibling's birth = dethronement; one parent = preference; misbehaviour = warning.
Adler stresses what is remembered; Freud stresses what is forgotten (repression).
Adler's false cemetery memory still symbolised fear, inferiority and overcoming them.

sections.heading: Dream Analysis
sections.detailed:
Adler agreed with Freud that dreams are valuable for understanding personality, but disagreed about how to interpret them. He did not think dreams fulfil wishes or reveal hidden conflicts. Instead, dreams involve our feelings about a current problem and what we intend to do about it.

Adler's own dream. Before his first trip to the United States, Adler was anxious about how he and his theory would be received. The night before sailing he dreamed the ship capsized and sank, destroying all his possessions; thrown into the sea, he struggled alone through choppy water but, through will and determination, finally reached land safely (Hoffman, 1994). The dream expressed his fear about what awaited him in America and his intention to land safely, that is, to succeed for himself and for individual psychology.

Present- and future-oriented. In the fantasies of dreams, both night dreams and daydreams, we believe we can overcome the hardest obstacle or simplify the most complex problem. Dreams therefore look toward the present and future, not toward past conflicts.

Interpretation. Adler insisted a dream should never be interpreted without knowing the person and their situation, because a dream expresses the person's style of life and is unique to them. Still, he did find common meanings for some dreams. Freud interpreted dreams of falling and flying sexually; Adler did not.
- Falling: a sense of demotion or loss, such as fear of losing self-esteem or prestige.
- Flying: striving upward, an ambitious style of life, a wish to be above or better than others.
- Flying and falling together: fear of being too ambitious and so failing.
- Being chased: a feeling of weakness relative to others.
- Being naked: fear of giving oneself away.

Table 4.1 (adapted from Grey, 1998) adds: being paralysed means facing insoluble problems; school exams mean being unprepared for situations; wearing the wrong clothes means being disturbed by one's faults; sexual themes mean retreating from sex or having inadequate information about it; rage indicates an angry or hostile style of life; and death indicates unresolved issues about the dead person.

On whether research supports this view (review question 17), studies discussed later found that dreaming helped people deal with a current threatening task and that people dream about the current problems they face.
sections.simple: Adler thought dreams are about our current problems and how we plan to handle them, not about hidden wishes from the past. He interpreted them only in the context of the dreamer's style of life, though some themes, like falling or flying, had typical meanings.
keyPoints: Dreams reflect feelings about a current problem and what we intend to do, not wish fulfilment.
Adler's shipwreck dream showed fear of America and determination to succeed.
Dreams are oriented to the present and future.
Interpret only with knowledge of the person; dreams express the style of life.
Falling = loss of esteem; flying = ambition; chased = weakness; naked = fear of giving oneself away.
Table 4.1: paralysis, exams, wrong clothes, sex, rage, death.

sections.heading: Measures of Social Interest
sections.detailed:
Adler himself did not want to use psychological tests to assess personality. He argued that tests create artificial situations that give ambiguous results, and that therapists should develop their intuition instead. He did support tests of memory and intelligence; it was personality tests he criticised.

Nevertheless, psychologists later developed tests to measure social interest and style of life.

Social Interest Scale (SIS) (Crandall, 1981). Made up of pairs of adjectives. Subjects choose the word in each pair describing an attribute they would like to have. Words such as helpful, sympathetic and considerate are taken to indicate social interest.

Social Interest Index (SII) (Greever, Tseng, & Friedland, 1973). A self-report inventory in which subjects rate how far statements describe them. Items, such as one about not minding helping out friends, were chosen to reflect Adler's ideas and to tap the ability to accept and cooperate with others. High scorers tend to be high in friendliness, empathy, cooperation, tolerance and independence, and lower in anxiety, hostility, depression and neuroticism (Leak, 2006a, 2006b).

Basic Adlerian Scales for Interpersonal Success (BASIS-A) (Peluso, Peluso, Buckner, Curlette, & Kern, 2004). A 65-item self-report inventory assessing lifestyle as well as social interest. It measures five dimensions: social interest, going along, taking charge, wanting recognition, and being cautious.

These tests made Adler's central health concept measurable and so opened the way to the social-interest research described later in the chapter.
sections.simple: Adler disliked personality tests, but later psychologists built three: the Social Interest Scale (adjective pairs), the Social Interest Index (self-report statements) and the BASIS-A (65 items covering lifestyle and social interest).
keyPoints: Adler rejected personality tests as artificial and ambiguous; preferred intuition (but accepted memory and IQ tests).
SIS (Crandall, 1981): choose preferred adjectives from pairs.
SII (Greever, Tseng, & Friedland, 1973): self-report statements about oneself.
High SII scorers: friendly, empathic, cooperative, tolerant; lower anxiety, hostility, depression, neuroticism.
BASIS-A: 65 items; social interest, going along, taking charge, wanting recognition, being cautious.

sections.heading: Research on Adler's Theory: Method, Dreams and Inferiority Feelings
sections.detailed:
Adler's method. Adler's primary research method was the case study, and little of his data survives. He published no case histories except two fragments: one written by a patient and one written by a patient's physician. He did not know these patients but analysed their personalities from their writings.

His data and method draw the same criticisms as Freud's and Jung's. His observations cannot be repeated or duplicated and were not made in a controlled, systematic way. He did not check the accuracy of patients' reports, did not explain how he analysed his data, and had no interest in the experimental method. One follower admitted that Adler wanted his psychology to be a science but that it has not been easily verified scientifically (Manaster, 2006).

Although most of Adler's propositions have resisted scientific validation, several have been researched: dreams, inferiority feelings, early recollections, pampering and neglect, social interest and birth order.

Dreams. Grieser, Greenberg and Harrison (1972) exposed subjects to a situation in which failing to solve a puzzle was a threat to the personality, then let them sleep. Some were allowed to dream (woken only from NREM sleep); others were woken during REM sleep so they could not dream. Those who dreamed later recalled significantly more of the unfinished puzzle, and the researchers concluded that dreaming helped subjects deal with the current threatening situation. Breger, Hunter and Lane (1971) studied college students expecting a stressful psychotherapy session and patients about to have major surgery; both groups dreamed about their conscious worries, fears and hopes, that is, the current problems they faced. Both studies support Adler's view that dreams concern present problems.

Inferiority feelings. Adults low in inferiority feelings tended to be more successful, self-confident and persistent in pursuing goals than those high in inferiority feelings. Among American college students, those with moderate inferiority feelings had higher grade point averages than those with low or high levels (Strano & Petrocelli, 2005). In China, Kosaka (2008) found that the focus of inferiority feelings shifts with age: younger teens felt inferior about poor grades, older teens about physical attractiveness, and college students about lack of social skills.
sections.simple: Adler relied on case studies that cannot be checked or repeated, so his theory is hard to test. Still, research supports his ideas that dreams deal with current problems and shows that inferiority feelings affect success, with moderate levels linked to the best grades.
keyPoints: Case study method; only two published fragments; unsystematic and unverifiable.
Researched topics: dreams, inferiority, early recollections, pampering, neglect, social interest, birth order.
Grieser et al. (1972): dreamers recalled more of the threatening unsolved puzzle.
Breger et al. (1971): people dream about current worries (therapy, surgery).
Strano & Petrocelli (2005): moderate inferiority = highest GPA.
Kosaka (2008): inferiority focus shifts from grades to looks to social skills with age.

sections.heading: Research on Early Recollections and The Nature of Early Recollections
sections.detailed:
Early recollections and clinical problems. Several studies show that early memories match people's current difficulties, as Adler predicted.
- Jackson and Sechrest (1962): early memories of anxiety neurotics concerned fear; of depressed people, abandonment; of people with psychosomatic complaints, illness.
- Hafner, Fakouri and Labrentz (1982): alcoholics' early memories contained threatening events and situations in which they were controlled by external circumstances rather than their own decisions; non-alcoholic controls showed neither theme.
- Patterson (2014): US police officers with traumatic early recollections had more pronounced PTSD symptoms than those without such memories.
- Hankoff (1987): adult criminals' early recollections dealt with disturbing or aggressive interactions and contained more unpleasant events than controls'.
- Davidow and Bruhn (1990): adolescent delinquents' early memories involved breaking rules, difficulty forming relationships and inability to cope alone; they saw parents as untrustworthy and more likely to hurt than help. Controls lacked these themes.
- Tobey and Bruhn (1992): psychiatric patients considered dangerous to themselves and others had more aggressive early memories than non-dangerous patients; they felt vulnerable and powerless and saw others as hostile and abusive.

The nature of early recollections. Research using objective scoring systems shows that early memories tend to be subjective recreations rather than events that really happened, much like Adler's cemetery memory (Statton & Wilborn, 1991). When people were asked to invent early recollections that might have happened to someone else, the themes resembled those of their own memories (Buchanan, Kern, & Bell-Dumas, 1991). This study supported Adler's claim that early recollections reveal one's current style of life and can therefore be used therapeutically.

Early recollections of adults in the United States and Israel also predicted career preferences. Physicists, mathematicians and psychologists recalled themes such as curiosity, independent thought and scepticism toward information from authority figures (Clark, 2005; Kasler & Nevo, 2005).

Table 4.2 (adapted from Bruhn, 1992) lists possible style-of-life themes: first school memory - attitudes to achievement, mastery and independence; first punishment memory - attitude toward authority; first sibling memory - sibling rivalry; first family memory - functioning in social situations; clearest memory of mother - attitudes toward women; clearest memory of father - attitudes toward men; memory of a person you admire - basis for role models; happiest memory - how your strongest needs are best gratified.
sections.simple: Research shows early memories reflect people's current problems: fear in anxious people, abandonment in depressed people, aggression in criminals and dangerous patients. These memories are often reconstructions rather than facts, but they still reveal the current style of life and even predict career choices.
keyPoints: Early memories match diagnoses: fear (anxiety), abandonment (depression), illness (psychosomatic).
Alcoholics, criminals, delinquents and dangerous patients show threatening or aggressive themes.
Traumatic early recollections linked to stronger PTSD in police officers.
Early recollections are subjective recreations (Statton & Wilborn, 1991).
Invented memories show the same themes as one's own (Buchanan et al., 1991).
Early recollections predict career preferences; Table 4.2 lists memory themes.

sections.heading: Research on Neglect and Pampering in Childhood
sections.detailed:
Neglect. Adler said neglected or rejected children develop feelings of worthlessness, and research supports him.
- Crook, Raskin and Eliot (1981): adults hospitalised for depression rated their parents as hostile, detached and rejecting; interviews with siblings, relatives and friends confirmed that the parents had indeed been hostile and neglectful.
- Lefkowitz and Tesiny (1984): parents of 8-year-olds reported their child-rearing behaviours and satisfaction with their children. Ten years later, at 18, the children took the MMPI depression scale. Those more depressed had been neglected by their parents; those whose parents had not been indifferent or unloving scored lower.
- More recent research (Bennett, Sullivan, & Lewis, 2010; Lowell et al., 2011; Milot et al., 2013): neglected children experience more shame, depression and PTSD symptoms and have poorer socialisation skills.
- Guan, Deng and Luo (2010): neglected Chinese children and adolescents aged 5-17 were far more likely to develop high anxiety.
- Widom et al. (2013): neglected children may be more prone to violence and excessive alcohol use later in life.
The chapter concludes that neglected children pay a high price as they grow up.

Pampering. Adler argued that pampering leads to a pampered style of life with little or no social feeling for others. Research supports this and suggests pampering can lead to excessive narcissism: lack of responsibility or empathy, an exaggerated sense of self-importance, and a tendency to exploit others. Studies identify four types of pampering:
1. Overindulgence - persistent parental gratification of the child's needs and wishes, leading to entitlement and tyrannical, manipulative behaviour.
2. Overpermissiveness - letting children do as they please with no thought for effects on others, leading to disregard for social rules and others' rights.
3. Overdomination - parents make all decisions, leading to low self-confidence and dependence on others in adulthood.
4. Overprotection - excessive parental caution and warnings about dangers, leading to generalised anxiety and avoidance of social situations.

Capron (2004) found that college students with over-domineering mothers were more likely to seek psychotherapy; students who saw their parents as both overindulgent and overprotective tended to have low self-esteem; and those whose parents were overindulgent and over-domineering scored high in narcissism.
sections.simple: Research backs Adler: neglected children grow up with more depression, anxiety, shame and later problems, while pampered children tend toward narcissism and low empathy. Researchers have identified four kinds of pampering: overindulgence, overpermissiveness, overdomination and overprotection.
keyPoints: Neglect linked to adult depression (Crook et al.; Lefkowitz & Tesiny).
Neglected children: more shame, depression, PTSD, anxiety, weaker social skills; later violence and alcohol use.
Pampering leads to narcissism: low empathy, self-importance, exploiting others.
Four types: overindulgence, overpermissiveness, overdomination, overprotection.
Capron (2004): parenting patterns linked to therapy-seeking, low self-esteem and narcissism.

sections.heading: Research on Social Interest
sections.detailed:
Research strongly supports Adler's claim that social interest goes with psychological health.

SIS research. People high in social interest reported less stress, depression, anxiety and hostility than those low in it, and scored higher on cooperation, empathy, responsibility and popularity (Crandall, 1984; Watkins, 1994; Watkins & St. John, 1994). College students high in social interest scored high in spirituality and religiosity, but of a positive, tolerant, helping kind, not religious ethnocentrism or fundamentalism (Leak, 2006a).

Well-being and purpose. Studies in the United States and China found high social interest linked to subjective well-being, hope and optimism, agreeableness, self-identity, self-determination and a strong sense of purpose in life (Barlow, Tobin, & Schmidt, 2009; Foley, Matheny, & Curlette, 2008; Leak & Leak, 2006).

Adolescents and offenders. High school students (grades 9-12) high in social interest had greater overall life satisfaction and satisfaction with friends and family (Gilman, 2001). Male criminal offenders aged 18-40 with high social interest were far less likely to reoffend after release (Daugherty, Murphy, & Paugh, 2001). Juvenile delinquents scored lower on social interest than non-delinquents (Newbauer & Stone, 2010).

SII research. Women high in social interest were significantly higher in self-actualisation, the healthy-personality characteristic described by Maslow. Social interest was higher in women than men and increased with age in both sexes (Greever, Tseng, & Friedland, 1973).

Culture. Among Latino men and women in the US, those well adjusted to both cultures scored higher on social interest than those acculturated mainly to only one lifestyle (Miranda, Frevert, & Kern, 1998).

Physical health. Social interest, with its sense of belonging, cooperation and contributing to or receiving support from a social network, is positively associated with physical and mental well-being. High scorers tended to have stronger immune systems, fewer colds, lower blood pressure and greater subjective well-being (Nikelly, 2005).

These findings answer review questions 9 and 18 on how high and low scorers differ.
sections.simple: People high in social interest are less stressed, anxious and depressed, more empathic and cooperative, happier and more satisfied with life, less likely to reoffend, and even physically healthier. Social interest is higher in women and grows with age.
keyPoints: High social interest: less stress, depression, anxiety, hostility; more cooperation, empathy, responsibility, popularity.
