sections.heading: Research on Birth Order: General Findings and First-Borns
sections.detailed:
A great deal of research has examined birth order (Eckstein & Kaufman, 2012).

General findings. A survey of 200 birth-order studies concluded that first-borns had higher success and achievement and were more likely to become accountants, lawyers, architects, surgeons, college professors or astronauts, while later-borns were more likely to become firefighters, high school teachers, musicians, photographers, social workers or stuntmen (Eckstein et al., 2010). Simply having older or younger siblings can matter: studies of nearly 20,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and about 3,500 in the US found that the number of older brothers a man had predicted his sexual orientation, with more older brothers linked to greater same-sex attraction; older sisters did not predict women's orientation (Bogaert, 2003). Birth order also affects choice of friends and romantic partners: people tend to associate with others of the same birth position, and only children with other only children (Hartshorne, 2010; Hartshorne et al., 2009).

First-borns: achievement and intelligence. In Finland, parents whose first child showed high intelligence, few behaviour problems and adaptability were more likely to have more children within 5 years (Jokela, 2010). Adler said first-borns are concerned with power and authority, which they can gain through work achievement. First-borns are over-represented from college to top management, more often become eminent, and attain greater academic achievement and career prestige (Breland, 1974; Schachter, 1963). In the US and Poland, first-borns scored higher on intelligence, completed more education and held more prestigious jobs (Herrera, Zajonc, Wieczorkowska, & Cichomski, 2003). In Sweden they scored higher on managerial or executive functioning (Holmgren, Molander, & Nilsson, 2006). Among 240,000+ Norwegian male recruits, older siblings outscored younger siblings on IQ (Kristensen & Bjerkedal, 2007). British research found first-borns far less likely than fifth-or-later children in large families to suffer PTSD, with later-borns more prone to stress and adjustment disorders (Green & Griffiths, 2014).

Not all researchers agree that first-borns are more intelligent (Rodgers, 2001). Belmont and Marolla (1973) analysed IQs of 400,000 European men and found a steady decline from first-borns to second-borns to third-borns and so on; Zajonc, Markus and Markus (1979) confirmed this for men and women in several nations. A possible explanation is not genetic but environmental: first-borns' exclusive early exposure to adults gives them a more stimulating intellectual environment. Yet first-borns do not always get better grades: US high school studies show first-borns have higher IQs but later-borns work harder and get higher GPAs (Frank, Turenshine, & Sullivan, 2010; Rettner, 2010).

First-borns: personality. First-borns tend to be more suggestible and dependent, anxious under stress, and higher in need for social relationships (Schachter, 1963, 1964), which fits Adler: dethroned first-borns try to regain position by conforming to parents' expectations, so they rely more on others' standards for behaviour and self-concept (Newman, Higgins, & Vookles, 1992). Other findings: first-borns lower in depression and anxiety and higher in self-esteem (Gates et al., 1988); possibly more extraverted and conscientious (Sulloway, 1995), though Dutch research found later-borns more extraverted, being more dominant and assertive (Pollet et al., 2010). First-born girls were more obedient, socially responsible and closer to parents (Sutton-Smith & Rosenberg, 1970). Studies in France, Croatia, Canada and England found first-borns more closely supervised, rated by mothers as less fearful, reporting more frightening childhood dreams, and scoring higher on dominance in college (Beck, Burnet, & Vosper, 2006; Begue & Roche, 2005; Kerestes, 2006; McCann, Stewin, & Short, 1990). Overall the results are described as generally supportive of Adler.
sections.simple: Research largely supports Adler on first-borns: they tend to achieve more, score higher on IQ, reach prestigious jobs and have higher self-esteem, though later-borns may work harder for grades. First-borns are also more suggestible, dependent and anxious under stress, as Adler's dethronement idea predicts.
keyPoints: First-borns: higher achievement, prestige, education and IQ in many countries.
Belmont & Marolla (1973): IQ declines with birth order; explained by exposure to adults, not genes.
Later-borns may work harder and earn higher GPAs.
First-borns: suggestible, dependent, anxious under stress (Schachter), rely on others' standards.
Mixed findings on extraversion (Sulloway vs Pollet et al.).
Number of older brothers predicts male sexual orientation (Bogaert); people befriend same birth position.

sections.heading: Research on Second-Born, Last-Born and Only Children; Birth-Order Effects: A Matter of Belief?
sections.detailed:
Second-born children. Less research exists on second-borns. A 3-year study of first- and second-born siblings found that second-borns' attitudes, personalities and leisure activities were influenced more by older siblings than by parents (McHale, Updegraff, Helms-Erikson, & Crouter, 2001). Among major league baseball players, younger brothers were 10 times more likely than older brothers to attempt the risky act of stealing bases, and had higher batting averages (Sulloway & Zweigenhaft, 2010).

Last-born children. Adler predicted that excessively pampered last-borns would have adjustment problems as adults. One popular explanation of alcoholism is an inability to cope with everyday demands, so Adler's theory predicts more alcoholism among last-borns than early-borns. Considerable research supports this. College binge drinking is significantly higher among last-borns than first-borns (Laird & Shelton, 2006), and last-borns may feel more academic rivalry with siblings (Badger & Reddy, 2009). The chapter's highlights box also notes last-borns tend to be high in social interest and agreeableness but can be rebellious.

Only children. Adler thought only-born adults are overly concerned with being the centre of attention and more selfish. Research has not consistently supported this. Falbo (1978) found only children more cooperative than first- or last-borns; Jiao, Ji and Jing (1986) found them more self-centred and less popular than children with siblings. An analysis of 115 studies found only-borns higher in achievement and intelligence and comparable in social and emotional adjustment (Falbo & Polit, 1986). Mellor (1990) confirmed this and found greater initiative, aspiration, industriousness and self-esteem. Only children are also strongly achievement-motivated and score high in confidence and organisational skills (Siribaddana, 2013). Across studies, the number of siblings consistently predicts educational success: fewer siblings, better school performance (Downey, 2001), possibly because only-borns get more educational opportunities and parental resources.

Birth-order effects: a matter of belief? After all these findings, the chapter adds one more study. People who believe in birth-order effects differ from those who do not: believers scored significantly lower in openness to new experiences and significantly higher in neuroticism (Gundersen, Brown, Bhathal, & Kennedy, 2011). This reminds students that belief in birth-order effects is itself related to personality.

These sections together answer review question 13: research on first-borns largely supports Adler, while research on only children only partly supports him, since only-borns often show high achievement and good adjustment rather than mere selfishness.
sections.simple: Second-borns are shaped more by older siblings and take more risks; last-borns binge-drink more, fitting Adler's pampering prediction. Research on only children is mixed and mostly positive (high achievement, self-esteem), contrary to Adler's view of them as selfish. Believers in birth-order effects are less open and more neurotic.
keyPoints: Second-borns influenced more by older siblings than parents (McHale et al., 2001); younger brothers steal more bases.
Last-borns: more binge drinking (Laird & Shelton, 2006), supporting Adler's alcoholism prediction.
Only children: mixed results on selfishness; high achievement, intelligence, self-esteem (Falbo & Polit; Mellor).
Fewer siblings predicts better educational success (Downey, 2001).
Believers in birth-order effects: lower openness, higher neuroticism (Gundersen et al., 2011).

sections.heading: Reflections on Adler's Theory: Contributions
sections.detailed:
Adler's influence on psychology has been substantial, making his theory one of the most enduring. He was ahead of his time: his cognitive and social emphases fit modern psychology better than the psychology of his own day (LaFountain, 2009). More than 30 years after Adler's death, Abraham Maslow wrote that Adler becomes more correct year by year, as the facts increasingly support his image of humanity.

Influence on other theorists.
- Karen Horney: Adler's emphasis on social forces appears in her theory (next chapter).
- Gordon Allport: Adler's focus on the whole person and the unity of personality is reflected in his work.
- Abraham Maslow: the creative power of people to shape their styles of life, and the view that future goals matter more than past events, influenced him.
- Julian Rotter, a social-learning theorist, wrote that he remained impressed by Adler's insights into human nature (Rotter, 1982).

Influence on psychoanalysis. Adler proposed an aggressive drive more than 12 years before Freud added aggression to sex as a primary motive. The neo-Freudian ego psychologists, who stress conscious and rational processes over the unconscious, follow Adler rather than Freud.

Views on women. Adler disputed Freud's view that women's supposed inferiority has a biological basis such as penis envy, calling this a myth invented by men to keep their sense of superiority. Women may feel inferior, he said, but because of social conditioning and sex-role stereotyping. He believed in equality of the sexes and supported women's emancipation movements.

Concepts of lasting importance. These include his early work on organic inferiority (which influenced the study of psychosomatic disorders), the inferiority complex, compensation and birth order. Adler is also regarded as a forerunner of social psychology and group therapy. Figure 4.1 notes that his books became very popular in the US and spawned the huge self-help genre.

This section answers review question 19 on Adler's contributions to psychology today.
sections.simple: Adler's ideas proved long-lasting and influenced Horney, Allport, Maslow and Rotter, as well as Freudian ego psychology. He proposed an aggressive drive before Freud, argued women's feelings of inferiority are social not biological, and gave psychology the inferiority complex, compensation and birth order.
keyPoints: Ahead of his time; cognitive and social emphases fit modern psychology; Maslow praised him.
Influenced Horney (social forces), Allport (unity of personality), Maslow (creative self, future goals) and Rotter.
Proposed an aggressive drive 12+ years before Freud; ego psychologists follow Adler.
Rejected penis envy; women's inferiority due to social conditioning; supported sex equality.
Lasting concepts: organic inferiority, inferiority complex, compensation, birth order; forerunner of social psychology and group therapy.

sections.heading: Reflections on Adler's Theory: Criticisms
sections.detailed:
Oversimplification. Freud charged that Adler's psychology was oversimplified and would appeal to many people precisely because it dropped the complicated unconscious, had no difficult concepts and ignored sex. Freud remarked that his own psychoanalysis took 2 years or more to learn, while Adler's ideas could be learned in two weeks because there was so little to know (quoted in Sterba, 1982). The chapter replies that the simplicity was deliberate: Adler wrote that it had taken him 40 years to make his psychology simple. The charge is reinforced by the fact that his books are easy to read, written for the general public, and some were compiled from popular lectures.

Reliance on common sense. A related charge is that Adler's concepts rely heavily on commonsense observations of everyday life. A New York Times book reviewer commented that no other eminent psychologist matched Adler's simplicity and non-technical language.

Inconsistency and gaps. Critics say Adler was inconsistent and unsystematic, leaving gaps and unanswered questions. Are inferiority feelings the only problem in life? Do all people strive primarily for perfection? Can we become reconciled to some inferiority and stop trying to compensate? Adler's system cannot answer all of these adequately, although the chapter notes that most theorists leave unanswered questions.

Determinism versus free will. Some psychologists question Adler's stance. Early in his career he did not oppose determinism, which was widely accepted in science and characterised Freud's theory. Later he wanted to give the self more autonomy, and his final formulation rejected determinism. The creative self proposes that before age 5 we fashion a style of life from the materials of heredity and environment, but it is not clear how a young child can make such momentous decisions. His preference for free will is clear; the specifics of how the style of life is formed are not.

Methodological criticisms from the research section also apply: case studies that cannot be repeated, unverified patient reports and no interest in experiments.
sections.simple: Critics, starting with Freud, called Adler's theory oversimplified and too close to common sense. Others say it is unsystematic with unanswered questions, and that it is unclear how a child under 5 could freely create a style of life.
keyPoints: Freud: oversimplified, learnable in two weeks; Adler said simplicity took 40 years.
Easy-to-read books for the public reinforce the charge.
Relies heavily on commonsense observation.
Inconsistent, unsystematic; gaps such as whether inferiority is the only problem.
Moved from determinism to free will; unclear how a child creates a style of life before age 5.

sections.heading: Later Recognition and Influence
sections.detailed:
Although his ideas have been widely accepted, Adler's public recognition declined after his death in 1937, and he has received relatively little later credit. Many of his concepts have been borrowed without acknowledgment.

A typical example: Freud's obituary in the Times of London named Freud as the originator of the term inferiority complex, and when Carl Jung died, the New York Times credited Jung with coining it. Neither newspaper mentioned Adler, the true originator. Adler did, however, receive one unusual honour: a British composer named a string quartet after him.

Adler's followers claim that individual psychology remains popular with psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers and educators. The North American Society of Adlerian Psychology publishes a quarterly journal, Individual Psychology: The Journal of Adlerian Theory, Research and Practice. Other Adlerian journals appear in Germany, Italy and France, and Adlerian training institutes exist in New York, Chicago and other cities. Figure 4.1 adds that his popular books in the US spawned the huge genre of self-help books.
sections.simple: After Adler died, his name faded even though his ideas spread; newspapers even credited Freud and Jung with his term inferiority complex. Still, Adlerian journals and training institutes continue today.
keyPoints: Recognition declined after 1937; ideas borrowed without credit.
Obituaries credited Freud and Jung with the term inferiority complex.
A British composer named a string quartet for Adler.
Quarterly journal Individual Psychology published by the North American Society of Adlerian Psychology.
Adlerian journals in Germany, Italy, France; institutes in New York, Chicago and elsewhere.

terms.definition: Adler's name for his theory of personality, stressing the uniqueness of each person and rejecting Freud's universal biological motives.
The normal, universal condition of all people, arising from infant helplessness; the source of all human striving.
The motivation to overcome real or imagined inferiority and strive toward higher levels of development.
A condition that develops when a person cannot compensate for normal inferiority feelings; marked by a poor self-opinion and feeling helpless before life's demands.
A defective organ or body part that shapes personality through the person's efforts to compensate for it; one of three sources of an inferiority complex.
Satisfying a child's every need and whim so that the child expects others to defer; can produce an inferiority complex when obstacles appear.
Lack of parental love and security from indifferent or hostile parents, producing worthlessness, anger and distrust; a source of an inferiority complex and now seen as a form of child abuse.
A condition that develops when a person overcompensates for normal inferiority feelings; an exaggerated opinion of one's abilities, with boasting, vanity and denigrating others.
Adler's early idea that people compensate for inferiority (equated with femininity) through a will to power in which aggression is central; later abandoned.
The innate, future-oriented urge toward perfection or completion that motivates each of us; Adler's 'fundamental fact of life'.
The idea that we have an ultimate goal or final state of being and a need to move toward it.
The idea that imagined or potential goals that cannot be tested against reality (above all the ideal of perfection) guide our behaviour.
Adler's preferred names for the concept known as fictional finalism.
A unique character structure or pattern of behaviours and characteristics by which each person strives for perfection; crystallised by age 4 or 5.
The ability to create an appropriate style of life from the materials provided by heredity and environment.
Style of life with a ruling attitude and little social awareness; extreme forms become sadists, delinquents or sociopaths, milder forms alcoholics, addicts or suicides.
Style of life that expects satisfaction from others and becomes dependent on them; the most common type according to Adler.
Style of life that makes no attempt to face problems, thereby avoiding any possibility of failure.
Healthy style of life that cooperates with others and copes with problems within a well-developed framework of social interest.
Our innate potential to cooperate with other people to achieve personal and societal goals; its development depends on early social experience.
Adler's German term for social interest, best translated as 'community feeling'.
A person's position among siblings; for Adler a major social influence in childhood from which the style of life is created.
The first-born's loss of the centre of attention and constant care when a second child arrives.
Adler's name for his primary assessment methods: order of birth, early recollections and dream analysis.
Assessment technique in which our earliest memories, whether of real events or fantasies, are assumed to reveal the primary interest of our life and our style of life.
Interpreting dreams as expressions of feelings about a current problem and what we intend to do about it, within the context of the dreamer's style of life.
Test of social interest using pairs of adjectives from which subjects choose the attribute they would like to possess (Crandall, 1981).
Self-report inventory in which subjects rate how well statements reflecting Adler's ideas describe them (Greever, Tseng, & Friedland, 1973).
Basic Adlerian Scales for Interpersonal Success: a 65-item self-report inventory measuring lifestyle and social interest on five dimensions.
Type of pampering: persistent parental gratification of a child's needs and desires, leading to entitlement and tyrannical, manipulative behaviour.
Type of pampering: letting children behave as they please without regard for others, leading to disregard of social rules and others' rights.
Type of pampering: exclusive parental decision-making, leading to lack of self-confidence and dependence on others in adulthood.
Type of pampering: excessive parental caution and warnings about danger, leading to generalised anxiety and avoidance of social situations.
Lack of responsibility or empathy for others, exaggerated self-importance and a tendency to exploit others; research links it to pampering.

people.name: Alfred Adler
people.contribution: Founder of individual psychology (1870-1937); proposed inferiority feelings, compensation, striving for superiority, style of life, creative self, social interest and birth order.

people.name: Sigmund Freud
people.contribution: Invited Adler to his discussion group in 1902; the two broke bitterly around 1911. Adler was never his disciple. Freud later called Adler's psychology oversimplified.

people.name: Sigmund (Adler's brother)
people.contribution: Adler's healthy, athletic older brother, later a wealthy businessman; Adler felt overshadowed by him all his life and was a typical competitive second-born.

people.name: Demosthenes
people.contribution: Ancient Greek statesman who overcame a stutter to become a great orator; an example of compensation for organic inferiority.

people.name: Theodore Roosevelt
people.contribution: Sickly child who became the 26th US president and a model of physical fitness; an example of compensation.

people.name: Hoffman
people.contribution: Adler biographer (1994) quoted on Adler's rise to American fame, his anger when his authority was challenged, his rivalry with his brother and his shipwreck dream.

people.name: Zajonc
people.contribution: Explained (2001) how first-borns gain verbal fluency by tutoring younger siblings; also coauthored research confirming birth-order IQ declines (Zajonc, Markus, & Markus, 1979).

people.name: Manaster
people.contribution: Adlerian who noted that Adler wanted a science but his psychology has not been easily verified scientifically; with Mays called early recollections the best single indicators of lifestyle.

people.name: Kopp and Eckstein
people.contribution: Contrasted Adler's focus on what is remembered (selective memory) with Freud's focus on what is forgotten through repression.

people.name: Crandall
people.contribution: Developed the Social Interest Scale (1981) and reported that high scorers have less stress, depression, anxiety and hostility.

people.name: Greever, Tseng, and Friedland
people.contribution: Developed the Social Interest Index (1973); found social interest higher in women, rising with age, and linked to self-actualisation in women.

people.name: Leak
people.contribution: Found high social interest linked to friendliness, empathy and lower anxiety and depression, and to tolerant, helping spirituality.

people.name: Bruhn
people.contribution: Developed the early memories procedure summarised in Table 4.2 and studied early memories of delinquents and dangerous patients.

people.name: Schachter
people.contribution: Found first-borns over-represented among high achievers and more suggestible, dependent, anxious under stress and needing social relationships.

people.name: Belmont and Marolla
people.contribution: Analysed IQs of 400,000 European men (1973), finding IQ declined from first-borns down through later-borns.

people.name: Sulloway
people.contribution: Suggested first-borns may be more extraverted and conscientious (1995); with Zweigenhaft found younger brothers stole more bases in baseball.

people.name: Falbo
people.contribution: Found only children more cooperative than first- or last-borns (1978); with Polit (1986) reviewed 115 studies showing only-borns high in achievement and intelligence.

people.name: Abraham Maslow
people.contribution: Wrote that Adler becomes more correct year by year; influenced by Adler's creative self and emphasis on future goals.

people.name: Karen Horney
people.contribution: Her theory reflects Adler's emphasis on social forces in personality.

people.name: Gordon Allport
people.contribution: His work reflects Adler's focus on the whole person and the unity of personality.

people.name: Julian Rotter
people.contribution: Social-learning theorist who said he remained impressed by Adler's insights into human nature.

people.name: LaFountain
people.contribution: Noted (2009) that Adler's cognitive and social emphases fit today's psychology better than that of his own time.

examples.title: Compensation: the stammering debater
examples.text: A Class 9 student who stammers joins the debate club and practises every evening until she wins the inter-school trophy. Adler would call this compensation for an organic inferiority, the same pattern as Demosthenes.

examples.title: Inferiority complex vs superiority complex
examples.text: Two boys fail the same entrance exam. One decides he is just not smart and stops trying (inferiority complex). The other tells everyone the exam was beneath him and mocks those who passed (superiority complex). Both are failing to compensate in a healthy way.

examples.title: Fictional finalism in daily life
examples.text: A student studies hard believing that 'hard work always pays off'. This cannot be proven true for every case, but the belief still guides her choices, which is what Adler meant by a fictional final goal.

examples.title: Dethronement at home
examples.text: A 3-year-old starts wetting the bed and throwing tantrums after a baby sister is born and relatives crowd around the newborn. Adler would see this as a dethroned first-born trying to win back the lost position.

examples.title: The four styles in a group project
examples.text: In a college group project, one member bosses everyone (dominant), one waits for others to do the work and takes credit (getting), one skips meetings to avoid blame (avoiding), and one divides tasks fairly and helps others (socially useful).

practice.answer: Compensation is the motivation to overcome real or imagined inferiority and to strive toward higher levels of development. Adler saw it as the healthy response to the universal inferiority feelings that begin in infancy; individual growth comes from compensation. For example, Demosthenes overcame a stutter to become a great orator.

Masculine protest was Adler's early term for compensating for inferiority, which he then equated with weakness or femininity, reflecting women's low status in his society. Its goal was a drive toward power in which aggression played a large part. Adler later abandoned it in favour of the broader idea of striving for superiority or perfection.

Dethronement is Adler's term for what happens to a first-born when a second child arrives: the first-born loses the centre of attention and constant love and must share parental affection. The first-born fights to regain the lost position but cannot succeed. The shock is greater for pampered first-borns and for those who are younger when the sibling arrives.

practice.q: If you could choose, which birth-order position would you pick, and why, in Adler's terms?
practice.answer: A strong answer applies Adler's descriptions. For example, choosing second-born: one would never suffer dethronement, would have relaxed parents and an older sibling as pacesetter, and would likely be optimistic, competitive and ambitious. The risk is underachieving if the older sibling seems unbeatable. Any choice should state both advantages and Adler's warned-of risks.

practice.q: Explain the concept of fictional finalism and how it relates to striving for superiority.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Adler used finalism for the idea that we have an ultimate goal, a final state of being, and a need to move toward it. Fictional finalism adds that these goals are imagined ideals, potentialities rather than actualities, which cannot be tested against reality.

Explanation: We live by ideals such as the belief that all people are created equal or basically good. Belief in rewards in an afterlife is not based on objective reality, yet it is real to the believer and shapes behaviour. Adler's own fictional goal was to conquer the death he faced at age 4, which he pursued by becoming a physician; it is fictional because death can never finally be beaten. The most pervasive fiction is the ideal of perfection, whose best formulation so far, Adler said, is the concept of God. He preferred the terms subjective final goal or guiding self-ideal.

Relation to striving for superiority: Striving for superiority is the innate, future-oriented drive toward perfection or completion, the fundamental fact of life. Fictional finalism names the kind of goal this striving pursues: perfection is an imagined ideal that can never be fully reached or proved, yet it pulls behaviour toward the future. Both concepts contrast with Freud's view that behaviour is determined by the past, and both imply that striving raises rather than reduces tension.

Conclusion: Fictional finalism explains how subjective ideals, above all perfection, guide the striving for superiority and make Adler's theory goal-directed and future-oriented.

practice.q: In what ways did Adler's theory reflect his own childhood and life experiences?
practice.answer:
Introduction: The chapter calls Adler's childhood a textbook example of his own theory of overcoming weakness and inferiority, and Adler said his views matched the facts of his childhood.

Inferiority and compensation: He suffered from rickets, was small and clumsy, and felt inferior to his healthy older brother and other children. He forced himself into games and sports and gained self-esteem, illustrating inferiority feelings and compensation, and later the idea of organic inferiority. At school he went from failing to top of the class through hard work.

Fictional goal: Nearly dying of pneumonia at 4 led him to decide to become a doctor; conquering death became his fictional final goal.

Family and birth order: Pampered and then dethroned at 2, and his father's favourite, he found the Oedipus complex foreign. As a second-born he competed all his life with his brother Sigmund, matching his description of competitive, ambitious second-borns. His sociability made peers and siblings central to his theory.

Power to social interest: While struggling inside Freud's circle he stressed power and dominance; after gaining recognition and mellowing, he stressed social interest.

Conclusion: Inferiority, compensation, fictional finalism, birth order and the shift to social interest all reflect Adler's life.

practice.q: Describe how Adler assessed the personalities of his patients.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Adler's aim was to discover the patient's style of life and decide whether it was appropriate. His sessions were informal, face to face in comfortable chairs, like chats between friends, and he used humour to help patients see how ridiculous their sickness was.

Observation: He noted how patients walked, sat, shook hands and chose a chair, believing body use reveals the style of life. Even sleeping positions were meaningful: lying flat or restless sleep means wanting to seem important; stomach sleeping a stubborn, negative personality; the fetal position fear of others; outstretched arms a need for support.

Entrance gates to mental life: (1) Order of birth, since position in the family shapes the style of life. (2) Early recollections from the first 4-5 years, real or imagined, which reveal the primary life interest; for example, memories of a sibling's birth show continuing dethronement. (3) Dream analysis, treating dreams as expressions of a current problem and intended solution, interpreted only in the context of the person's style of life.

Tests: Adler disliked personality tests, but later psychologists created the SIS, SII and BASIS-A to measure social interest and lifestyle.

Conclusion: Adler's assessment was holistic and intuitive, centred on uncovering the style of life.

practice.q: What is the importance of early recollections in personality assessment? Give an example from Adler's own life.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Adler held that personality is formed in the first 4 or 5 years, so memories from that period reveal the style of life that continues into adulthood. Whether a memory is real or fantasy makes little difference, because either way it reflects the person's primary interest; early recollections were called the most satisfactory single indicators of lifestyle.

Interpretation: Memories of danger or punishment suggest hostility; of a sibling's birth, continuing dethronement; of one parent, preference for that parent; of misbehaviour, a warning not to repeat it. Adler stressed selective memory, what is remembered, whereas Freud stressed what is forgotten through repression.

Adler's example: At age 5 he remembered being terrified of a cemetery on his way to school and running through it a dozen times to conquer his fear. Thirty years later classmates told him there had never been a cemetery. The memory was false, yet it captured the fear, inferiority and determined effort to overcome them that defined his style of life.

Research support: Early memories match diagnoses (Jackson & Sechrest, 1962), are often subjective recreations (Statton & Wilborn, 1991), and predict career preferences (Clark, 2005; Kasler & Nevo, 2005).

Conclusion: Early recollections are a key entrance gate to the style of life.

practice.q: What is the purpose of dreams for Adler? Does research support his view?
practice.answer:
Adler's view: Adler agreed with Freud that dreams help us understand personality but rejected the idea that they fulfil wishes or reveal hidden conflicts. Dreams express feelings about a current problem and what we intend to do about it. In dreams we feel able to surmount any obstacle, so dreams are oriented to the present and future. His own dream before his first US trip, of surviving a shipwreck by sheer determination, showed his fear and his intention to succeed.

Interpretation: Dreams must be read in the context of the dreamer's style of life, but some themes recur: falling shows fear of losing esteem; flying, an ambitious style; flying then falling, fear of overambition; being chased, weakness relative to others; nakedness, fear of giving oneself away. Table 4.1 adds paralysis (insoluble problems), exams (unpreparedness) and rage (hostile style).

Research: Grieser, Greenberg and Harrison (1972) found that subjects allowed to dream after failing an ego-threatening puzzle recalled more of it than those woken in REM sleep, suggesting dreaming helps deal with current threats. Breger, Hunter and Lane (1971) found students facing stressful therapy and patients facing surgery dreamed about their current worries.

Conclusion: Research generally supports Adler's view that dreams address current problems.

practice.q: How do people high in social interest differ from those low in social interest?
practice.answer:
Introduction: Social interest is the innate potential to cooperate with others to achieve personal and societal goals. It is measured by the SIS (choosing preferred adjectives such as helpful or considerate), the SII (rating self-descriptive statements) and the 65-item BASIS-A. Adler regarded it as the yardstick of mental health: the socially useful type has it, while the dominant, getting and avoiding types lack it.

Emotional health: High scorers report less stress, depression, anxiety, hostility and neuroticism (Crandall, 1984; Leak, 2006). They are more friendly, empathic, cooperative, tolerant, responsible and popular.

Well-being and values: They show greater subjective well-being, hope, optimism, agreeableness, self-determination and purpose in life, and a tolerant, helping spirituality. Women high in social interest are higher in self-actualisation; social interest is higher in women and rises with age.

Behaviour: High school students high in social interest are more satisfied with life, friends and family (Gilman, 2001); offenders high in it are far less likely to reoffend (Daugherty et al., 2001); delinquents score lower (Newbauer & Stone, 2010). Biculturally adjusted Latinos score higher.

Health: High scorers have stronger immune systems, fewer colds and lower blood pressure (Nikelly, 2005).

Conclusion: Research supports Adler's claim that social interest is the mark of a healthy personality.

practice.q: Discuss the contributions and criticisms of Adler's theory.
practice.answer:
Contributions: Adler was ahead of his time; his cognitive and social emphases fit modern psychology, and Maslow said he became more correct year by year. His emphasis on social forces influenced Horney, his focus on the unity of personality influenced Allport, and the creative self and future goals influenced Maslow; Rotter praised his insights. He proposed an aggressive drive 12 years before Freud, and ego psychologists follow his emphasis on conscious processes. He rejected penis envy, explained women's inferiority as social conditioning and supported equality. Lasting concepts include organic inferiority (influencing psychosomatic research), the inferiority complex, compensation and birth order; he was a forerunner of social psychology and group therapy, and his books spawned self-help literature.

Criticisms: Freud called his theory oversimplified, learnable in two weeks, though Adler said simplicity took 40 years. His concepts rely on common sense. He was inconsistent and unsystematic, leaving questions such as whether inferiority is the only problem. It is unclear how a child under 5 could create a style of life. His case-study data cannot be verified or replicated.

Balance: The chapter notes that most theorists leave unanswered questions, and that research has supported several Adlerian ideas, such as early recollections, the effects of neglect and pampering, social interest and first-born achievement, even though most of his propositions resist scientific validation.

Conclusion: Despite weaknesses, Adler's theory remains one of the most enduring, even though he received little public credit after 1937.

practice.q: Explain Adler's concepts of inferiority feelings, the inferiority complex, the superiority complex and striving for superiority. How do they differ?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Alfred Adler's individual psychology places inferiority at the root of human motivation. Four related concepts must be carefully distinguished: inferiority feelings, the inferiority complex, the superiority complex and striving for superiority. Together they explain both healthy growth and maladjustment.

Inferiority feelings

Adler held that to be human is to feel inferior. Inferiority feelings are the normal condition of all people and a constant motivating force behind all behaviour, so they are not a sign of weakness or abnormality. They begin in infancy, when the child is small, helpless and dependent and is aware of the greater power of adults. This early inferiority is not genetic but arises from the environment of helplessness that all infants share. These feelings are inescapable and necessary, because they motivate compensation: efforts to overcome real or imagined inferiority and strive toward higher development. All individual growth results from compensation.

The inferiority complex

If a child cannot compensate, inferiority feelings intensify into an inferiority complex. The person has a poor self-opinion and feels helpless and unable to cope with life's demands. Adler found it in the childhood of many of his adult patients and named three sources. Organic inferiority: a defective organ or body part may lead to compensation, as with Demosthenes overcoming a stutter, Theodore Roosevelt becoming physically fit, or the circus performers among Adler's patients; but failed compensation produces a complex. Spoiling: pampered children expect everyone to defer to them, are shocked at school, lack social feeling and, when blocked, decide they must have some personal deficiency. Neglect: unloved, rejected children feel worthless, angry and distrustful; neglect is now recognised as child abuse.

The superiority complex

A person may overcompensate and develop a superiority complex, an exaggerated opinion of their abilities and accomplishments. Some feel inwardly superior without needing real achievement; others work very hard to become extremely successful. Both tend toward boasting, vanity, self-centredness and denigrating others.

Striving for superiority

Adler's early idea was the masculine protest, compensation for weakness equated with femininity through a drive for power and aggression. He later replaced it with striving for superiority or perfection, the fundamental fact of life. This has nothing to do with the superiority complex: it is not an attempt to be better than others or an inflated self-image, but a drive to perfect oneself, to become complete or whole (perfection comes from a Latin word meaning to complete). It is innate and future-oriented, unlike Freud's past-determined view. It increases rather than reduces tension, and it operates both in individuals and in society, which strives to perfect its culture. It is guided by fictional finalism, imagined ideals such as perfection.

Key differences

Inferiority feelings are normal and motivating; the inferiority complex is failure to compensate; the superiority complex is overcompensation; striving for superiority is the healthy, universal goal of completion. The first and last are universal and healthy, while the two complexes are maladaptive outcomes.

Conclusion

These concepts show that, for Adler, feeling inferior is the starting point of all growth. Whether it leads to healthy striving toward perfection or to a complex depends on compensation, which in turn depends on early experiences such as physical health, pampering and neglect.

practice.q: Describe Adler's views on birth order and evaluate them in the light of research.
practice.answer:
Introduction

One of Adler's most enduring contributions is that birth order is a major social influence from which we create our style of life. Siblings share parents and a home but not identical social environments, since being older or younger and meeting different parental attitudes create different conditions. Adler described four positions.

First-born

First-borns get undivided attention until a second child dethrones them. They fight to regain their position, may become stubborn and destructive and may hate the newcomer, but the battle is lost. Pampered first-borns, and those who are younger when the sibling arrives, suffer more. First-borns tend to be past-oriented, nostalgic, pessimistic and concerned with power, order and authority; they are good organisers, conscientious, authoritarian and conservative (Adler called Freud a typical eldest son). Tutoring younger siblings gives them an intellectual edge (Zajonc). They may also become insecure and hostile; Adler thought neurotics and criminals were often first-borns.

Second-born

Second-borns never hold power or suffer dethronement, and parents are more relaxed. The older sibling is a pacesetter, model and rival, so they tend to be optimistic, competitive and ambitious, like Adler with his brother Sigmund. If the older sibling seems unbeatable, they may underachieve.

Youngest and only child

Youngest children are never dethroned, are often the family pet, and, driven to surpass siblings, develop quickly and achieve highly; but excessive pampering may leave them helpless and dependent. Only children stay the centre of attention and mature early through time with adults, but learn neither to share nor to compete and are disappointed when not the focus. Adler stressed these are likelihoods, not firm rules; the creative self uses birth order with social interactions.

Research evaluation

First-borns: findings largely support Adler. They are over-represented among high achievers and eminent people (Breland; Schachter), score higher on intelligence and education (Herrera et al., 2003), executive functioning and IQ (Kristensen & Bjerkedal, 2007). Belmont and Marolla (1973) found IQ declining with birth order in 400,000 men, perhaps because first-borns have exclusive adult contact. They are more suggestible, dependent and anxious under stress (Schachter), fitting conformity after dethronement, and higher in self-esteem with less depression (Gates et al., 1988). However, later-borns may work harder for higher GPAs, and findings on extraversion conflict.

Second-borns are influenced more by older siblings than parents (McHale et al., 2001) and take more risks in baseball. Last-borns show more binge drinking (Laird & Shelton, 2006), supporting Adler's prediction about pampered last-borns. Only children give mixed results: Falbo (1978) found them more cooperative, Jiao et al. (1986) more self-centred, and reviews show higher achievement, intelligence and self-esteem with normal adjustment (Falbo & Polit, 1986; Mellor, 1990), only partly supporting Adler. Finally, believers in birth-order effects are less open and more neurotic (Gundersen et al., 2011).

Conclusion

Adler's birth-order ideas have generated a large body of research that broadly supports his views on first-borns and last-borns, while only-child findings are more positive than he predicted.

practice.q: Compare Adler's image of human nature with Freud's, and explain the roles of the style of life, the creative power of the self and social interest.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Adler and Freud grew up in the same city and era and trained at the same university, yet produced very different theories. Adler's individual psychology presents a hopeful, flattering view of people that the chapter calls the antithesis of Freud's pessimism.

Points of difference

First, Freud saw sex as primary; Adler minimised it and saw people as social beings shaped by social interactions. Second, Freud put the unconscious at the core; Adler put the conscious. Third, Freud held behaviour determined by the past; Adler stressed future goals, the striving for superiority and fictional finalism. Fourth, Freud saw motivation as tension reduction; Adler said striving increases tension. Fifth, Freud offered universality and sameness; Adler stressed uniqueness. Sixth, Freud's view was deterministic; Adler stressed free will. Adler also rejected the Oedipus complex and penis envy, and emphasised siblings and peers.

Style of life

Each person strives for perfection in a unique way, the style of life: a pattern of characteristics and behaviours developed while compensating for childhood inferiority. It shapes what we notice and what attitudes we hold, is learned socially, especially through birth order and the parent-child relationship, and is crystallised by age 4 or 5. Adler described four basic styles for the problems of social relations, occupation and love: dominant, getting (most common), avoiding and socially useful.

Creative power of the self

An early-fixed style of life seems as deterministic as Freud's theory. Adler resolved this with the creative self: we create our personality, using heredity and environment as raw materials. Our conscious attitude to experiences matters more than the experiences. People thus play an active role in developing the self, though once formed the style of life remains constant.

Social interest

Social interest is the innate potential to cooperate with others for personal and social goals (Gemeinschaftsgefuhl, community feeling). Its development depends on early experience, especially the mother, who must teach cooperation, companionship and courage. Only the socially useful type has well-developed social interest; the other three types lack it and are prone to neurosis and psychosis.

Human nature summary

On the basic issues, Adler favours free will, uniqueness, a balance of innate potentials (social interest, striving) realised through experience, a past that matters but does not trap us, and optimism about individuals and society.

Assessment and therapy

The contrast extends to practice. Freud's patients lay on a couch with the analyst out of sight; Adler sat facing patients in comfortable chairs, used friendly humour, and read the style of life from posture, handshakes and even sleeping positions. Freud interpreted dreams as disguised wishes from the past; Adler saw them as attempts to deal with current problems. Freud stressed what is forgotten through repression; Adler stressed what is remembered in early recollections, because selective memories support one's present direction of striving.

Conclusion

Adler's style of life, creative self and social interest together express a conscious, social, free and future-oriented view of people, the opposite of Freud's instinct-driven and pessimistic picture, and help explain Adler's influence on later humanistic and social theorists.

summary: Adler's individual psychology stresses each person's uniqueness, social rather than biological forces, and the conscious mind; it minimises sex.
His childhood of rickets, near death, dethronement and rivalry with an older brother is a textbook example of his own theory of compensating for inferiority.
Adler spent 9 years in Freud's circle but was never his disciple; after a bitter split he founded the Society for Individual Psychology (1912) and became America's first popular psychologist.
Inferiority feelings are universal, arise from infant helplessness, and are the source of all striving through compensation.
Failure to compensate produces an inferiority complex, arising from organic inferiority, spoiling or neglect; overcompensation produces a superiority complex.

The ultimate goal is striving for superiority or perfection (completion), which is future-oriented, increases tension, and operates in individuals and society; it replaced Adler's early idea of the masculine protest.
Fictional finalism: imagined, untestable ideals, above all perfection, guide behaviour.

The style of life is the unique way each person strives for perfection, learned socially and fixed by age 4 or 5; the creative power of the self means we build it ourselves from heredity and environment.
Four styles of life: dominant, getting (most common), avoiding and socially useful; only the last has social interest.
Social interest is an innate potential to cooperate, developed through early experience, especially the mother, who teaches cooperation, companionship and courage.

Birth order: first-borns are dethroned and become past-oriented and concerned with authority; second-borns are competitive and ambitious; youngest children may achieve highly or stay dependent; only children mature early but cannot share or compete.
Adler's image of human nature is optimistic: free will, uniqueness, innate potentials shaped by experience, and no victimhood to childhood.
Assessment used the entrance gates of birth order, early recollections and dream analysis; later tests (SIS, SII, BASIS-A) measure social interest.

Research supports Adler on dreams, early recollections, neglect, pampering, social interest and well-being, first-borns' achievement and dependence, and last-borns' drinking; findings on only children are mixed.
Adler influenced Horney, Allport, Maslow, Rotter and ego psychology, but was criticised as oversimplified, commonsense and unsystematic, and received little public credit after 1937.

assessment.explain: The less virulent dominant types become alcoholics, addicts or suicides, believing they hurt others by attacking themselves (p. 115).

assessment.explain: Adler traced evils from war to racial hatred to public drunkenness to a lack of community feeling (p. 116).
